**Too much social media? Unveiling the effects of determinants in social media fatigue** (URL: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11300332/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11300332/))  
*(Published July 2024\)*

* Study aim: explore antecedents of social media fatigue, including social media helpfulness, social media self-efficacy, online subjective well-being, social comparison, compulsive social media use, privacy concerns, FoMO, and information overload & to further discuss determinants of social media fatigue on social anxiety and lurking  
* Methods: distributed online questionnaire to social media users. 659 valid responses  
    * Purposively selected participants through social media platforms known for high levels of user engagement (like Facebook, Instagram, & Twitter) based on their SMU patterns, and targeted individuals who “exhibited behaviors indicative of potential susceptibility to social media fatigue”  
    * Measurement scale was a seven-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree”  
* Theoretical framework:  
    * Cognitive load theory: “suggests individuals have a finite capacity for processing information”  
        * In social media, users often encounter overwhelming amount of info, resulting in cognitive overload and fatigue  
    * Social comparison theory: “asserts that people assess their social & personal worth by comparing themselves to others”  
        * On social media, frequent comparison can lead to negative self-assessments & fatigue  
    * Social cognitive theory: “indicates an individual’s confidence in coping w/ life stress and achieving performance”  
        * Supports the social media self-efficacy antecedents of research (social media helpfulness, social media self-efficacy, online subjective well-being, social comparison, compulsive social media use, privacy concerns, FoMO, & information overload)  
* Social media fatigue \-\> “excessive & compulsive use of social media, or perceived information overload on social media, may lead to users becoming tired of social media activity”  
    * Users are exposed to excessive & ambiguous information on social media  
    * Harmful to both users and service providers  
    * May lead to negative psychological effects on users (like depression, anxiety, emotional stress, & social anxiety)  
* Social media helpfulness \-\> “refers to the extent to which users receive resources & useful information from exploring social media”  
    * May satisfy needs such as communicating w/ others, finding friends, keeping up-to-date, and entertainment   
* Self efficacy defined as “the belief that an individual can organize and perform a specific action”  
    * Can also be thought of as an individual’s confidence in coping w/ life stress & achieving performance   
    * Has been pointed out that people w/ high confidence are more likely to take action and stick with it, and they are also willing to adopt new technologies or search for useful information  
    * Research has found that media use experience has positive effect on self-efficacy   
        * As a result, users’ perceived ability to use social media increases \-\> willingness to share info increases \-\> happier feelings  
    * Suggests users are less likely to experience social media fatigue when they perceive social media self-efficacy  
* Subjective well-being defined as “broad phenomenon that includes people’s emotional responses, domain satisfaction, and overall judgements of life satisfaction”  
    * Important components: emotional well-being (assesses individual’s mood) & cognitive well-being (measures individual’s life satisfaction)  
    * Popularity of information & communication technology in the media has improved people’s well-being but also occupies time when people maintain relationships w/ friends (which indirectly has negative impact on subjective well-being)  
* Online subjective well-being defined as “the broad range of feelings & emotions experienced by individuals using the internet & social media such as satisfaction, well-being, and negative and positive affect”  
    * Previous studies found that individuals who perceived higher online subjective well-being may experience lower fatigue due to their ability to properly balance and process social media communications  
    * Previous studies mention that life satisfaction & subjective well-being are negatively correlated w/ adverse social media use symptoms   
    * Users’ satisfaction & high perceived benefits from social media may enable them to have higher cognitive processing ability to deal with info/content on social media, thereby experiencing low social media fatigue  
* Social comparison theory implications  
    * If users of social media cannot have a perception of their abilities, they will compare themselves to others when confronted w/ info about others (e.g., occupations, abilities, & achievements)  
    * Studies exploring social media have shown that individuals tend to make more negative social comparisons \-\> can lead to decreased well-being   
    * Sharing content on social media to positively present people favorably can lead others to see distorted version of their lives  
* Compulsive behavior/use \-\> repetitive addiction (like excessive use of online social media) that can have negative personal & social consequences  
    * Masur et al. (2014) found that social media addiction often leads to wasted time, reduced social connections, lower work & school performance, loss of control, and withdrawal syndrome  
    * Compulsive social media use is one of the major contributors to social media fatigue  
* Personal privacy concerns refer to “fear that one’s personal information will be collected and misused by others, and cannot be fully protected”  
    * According to previous studies, people who are highly concerned about privacy are prone to social media fatigue  
    * People w/ high social media self-efficacy “tend to perceive the helpfulness of social media, and at the same time they will become more and more aware of privacy concerns, leading to social media fatigue”  
* Fear of missing out (FoMO) defined as “worry or fear of being disconnected, absent, or missing out on experiences that others (e.g., peers, friends, family) might have or enjoy  
    * When experiencing it, people may be eagerly seeking & acknowledging others’ activities   
    * It is one of the important stressors that put social media users under mental and emotional stress  
* Information overload defined as “a situation in which a large amount of input information exceeds the information processing capacity of an individual”  
    * Occurs when people are exposed to more info than they can process efficiently  
    * Large amounts of info can be generated & disseminated rapidly on social media  
    * It may trigger user fatigue  
* Consequences of social media fatigue:  
    * Social anxiety refers to “the pervasive and debilitating experience of discomfort and avoidance of interpersonal interactions due to the fear of being negatively judged, rejected, or embarrassed”  
        * Closely related to mobile phone addiction  
        * “Scholars believe that when experiencing fatigue, users’ cognitive abilities decline, thereby predisposing them to inadequate regulation and control of emotions and attention, such as anxiety”  
        * Alkis et al. (2017) “developed & verified the social anxiety scale of social media users, and found that undergraduate students have social anxiety caused by social media, and have higher social anxiety for SNS”  
    * Lurking is “associated with non-posting behavior and is defined as inactive online user behavior”  
        * Lurkers rarely post, are silent, do not participate, or have not been involved and contributed to online activities  
        * Some users who find it difficult to adapt to the diversity of social media may overload their info, making users unable to cope effectively & choose to be lurkers  
        * Perceived by users as safer & easier social strategy for coping w/ distress  
        * May act as a “maladaptive countermeasure to reduce short-term stress at the expense of increasing long-term stress”  
        * Researchers have found that “social media fatigue may be an important driver of discontinuous use intentions”  
* Results of hypothesis testing:  
    * Social media self-efficacy had a negative significant effect on social media fatigue  
    * Compulsive social media use, FoMO, and information overload had a positive significant effect on social media fatigue  
    * Social media helpfulness, online subjective well-being, social comparison, and privacy concerns had no significant effect on social media fatigue  
    * Social media fatigue had a positive and significant effect on social anxiety and lurking  
    ![][image1]  
* Indirect relationships:  
    * SC and HF did not have significant indirect relationships with SA, while having SMF as a mediator  
    * SE, CSMU, FoMO, and IO were found to significantly impact SA indirectly via SMF  
    * OSWB, PC, SC, and HF did not indirectly impact LU, while having SMF as a mediator  
    * SE, CSMU, FoMO, and IO were found to have significant indirect relationships with LU via SMF  
    *HF, Social Media Helpfulness; SE, Self-Efficacy; OSWB, Online Subjective Well-Being; SC, Social Comparison; CSMU, Compulsive Social Media Use; PC, Privacy Concerns; FOMO, Fear of Missing Out; IO, Information Overload; SMF, Social Media Fatigue; SA, Social Anxiety; LU, Lurking.*  
* Summary:  
    * While enjoying the benefits of online communication, many young individuals are experiencing various challenges such as negative comparisons, too much information, and difficulties interacting with others  
    * **Social media self-efficacy was found to have a significant negative impact on social media fatigue**  
    * **Compulsive social media use and FoMO had significant positive impacts on social media fatigue**  
    * **Information overload has a significant positive impact on social media fatigue**  
        * **However, the chronic fear and stress of not having the same experience of others once withdrawing from social media can also lead to fatigue**  
    * **Social media helpfulness had no impact on social media fatigue**  
    * **Social comparison had no significant impact on social media fatigue**  
    * **Impact of privacy concerns on social media fatigue was not significant**  
    * **Social media fatigue had a positive and significant impact on social anxiety**  
        * **Furthermore, FoMO mediated the anxiety-social media fatigue association across dimensions**  
    * **Social media fatigue was found to significantly impact lurking**
